title: Chemistry IX · 2024 · E-Marking Notes (Questions & Solved Better Responses)
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This comprehensive digital E-Marking guide is compiled for secondary educators and students preparing for AKU-EB SSC-I Chemistry examinations. It provides rigorous question-by-question performance breakdowns, marking schemes, common student misconceptions, better responses, examiner suggestions, and complete model answers for the 2024 Annual Theory Examination Paper II.
generalObservations: Overall candidate performance in SSC-I Chemistry 2024 demonstrated solid foundational knowledge in stoichiometric mole calculations, periodic table classification, and atomic structure. Key areas requiring pedagogical reinforcement include distinguishing subtle characteristics in non-linear solubility curves, drawing coordinate covalent electron-dot structures, and mastering balanced half-reactions in commercial dry cells.

questions.questionText:
An element X of period 3 with atomic mass 27 amu carries 3 electrons in its valence shell.
Calculate its number of electrons, protons and neutrons if atom X loses all of its valence electrons.
questions.sloText: Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in atoms and ions;
checkingHints: 1 mark for determining the correct number of protons (13 protons).
1 mark for calculating electrons in the cation after loss of 3 valence electrons (13 - 3 = 10 electrons).
1 mark for calculating neutrons: 27 - 13 = 14 neutrons.
questions.overallPerformance: A significant majority of candidates performed well on this question. Successful candidates accurately mapped Period 3 with 3 valence electrons to Aluminum (Z = 13, A = 27) and correctly adjusted the electron count for ion formation.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses systematically stated the element as Aluminum (Z = 13), recognized that the nuclear proton count remains constant at 13, calculated electrons as 13 - 3 = 10 for the Al3+ ion, and calculated neutrons as 27 - 13 = 14.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses confused protons with electrons, often subtracting 3 from the proton number (stating 10 protons), or subtracted mass number from atomic number resulting in negative or inverted neutron counts.
suggestions: Emphasize that chemical reactions and ionization only involve transfer or sharing of valence electrons; nuclear composition (protons and neutrons) is strictly unaffected.
Provide regular structured practice linking periodic table coordinates (Period and Group) to atomic number, atomic mass, and subatomic composition.
questions.modelAnswer:
Element Identification:
- Element X in Period 3 with 3 valence electrons is Aluminum (Z = 13, A = 27 amu).

Subatomic Particles after losing all 3 valence electrons (Al3+ ion):
• Number of protons = 13 (determined by atomic number Z, which is unaffected by electron loss)
• Number of electrons = 13 - 3 = 10 electrons
• Number of neutrons = A - Z = 27 - 13 = 14 neutrons

questions.questionText:
Complete the given table by choosing the correct element for each property from the following list.
• Fluorine
• Sodium
• Sulphur
• Carbon
• Oxygen
• Helium

1. It produces a basic oxide on reaction with oxygen.
2. It is an unreactive, colourless gas.
3. It has an oxidation state of negative one.
questions.sloText: Identify elements and periodic properties based on oxide nature, reactivity, and oxidation states;
checkingHints: 1 mark for correctly matching Property 1 with Sodium (Na).
1 mark for correctly matching Property 2 with Helium (He).
1 mark for correctly matching Property 3 with Fluorine (F).
questions.overallPerformance: Performance was generally strong. Most candidates easily identified Helium as an unreactive gas and Sodium as forming a basic oxide, though some struggled between Fluorine and Oxygen for the -1 oxidation state.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly selected Sodium for basic oxide (Na2O), Helium for unreactive monoatomic noble gas, and Fluorine for constant -1 oxidation state.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses chose Carbon or Sulphur for basic oxide (confusing non-metal acidic oxides with basic metal oxides) or selected Oxygen for -1 oxidation state (which is normally -2 in oxides, except in peroxides).
suggestions: Reinforce the classification of element oxides: metals form basic oxides while non-metals form acidic or neutral oxides.
Clarify rules for oxidation numbers: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and is assigned -1 in all its compounds.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It produces a basic oxide on reaction with oxygen: Sodium
2. It is an unreactive, colourless gas: Helium
3. It has an oxidation state of negative one: Fluorine

questions.questionText:
a. Describe the movement of particles in liquid state. (1 Mark)
b. If the liquid is exposed to cold temperatures, what will be the effect on the movement of particles? (1 Mark)
c. If the same number of particles of a gas and liquid are placed in a container at standard temperature and pressure, then why the volume of the gas is found to be greater than that of liquid? (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Explain the kinetic molecular theory of matter across states and phase changes;
checkingHints: 1 mark for describing liquid particle motion (random motion, sliding/flowing over one another while staying in contact).
1 mark for stating that cooling reduces kinetic energy, causing particle motion to slow down.
1 mark for explaining that gas volume is greater because gas particles have negligible attraction and very large intermolecular spaces.
questions.overallPerformance: Most candidates demonstrated satisfactory qualitative understanding of particle motion in liquids and the cooling effect, but part (c) saw incomplete answers that failed to mention intermolecular spaces.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses articulated that liquid particles glide past each other in continuous contact, that cooling decreases average kinetic energy and velocity, and that gases occupy more volume because intermolecular forces are negligible and intermolecular spaces are huge.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses vaguely stated that particles 'stop moving' on cooling, or simply stated 'gas is lighter' without discussing intermolecular spaces or intermolecular forces.
suggestions: Use molecular animations showing particle spacing and movement in solids, liquids, and gases under varying temperatures.
Emphasize the explicit relationship between temperature and average kinetic energy (KE = 1/2 m v^2).
questions.currentTopic: Structure of Molecules & States of Matter
questions.modelAnswer:
a. In the liquid state, particles are in continuous, random motion, sliding, rolling, and flowing past each other while remaining in close contact.
b. When cooled, the average kinetic energy of the particles decreases, causing their movement to slow down and particles to draw closer together.
c. In a gas, intermolecular forces of attraction are negligible and intermolecular empty spaces between particles are extremely large compared to liquids, so the same number of particles disperses to occupy a vastly larger volume.

questions.questionText:
Give a reason why metals:
a. have high melting points. (1 Mark)
b. are good conductors of electricity. (1 Mark)
c. are malleable and ductile. (1 Mark)
d. are lustrous. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Explain physical properties of metals in terms of metallic bonding and delocalised electrons;
checkingHints: 1 mark for linking high melting points to strong electrostatic attractions in the metallic lattice.
1 mark for attributing electrical conductivity to mobile delocalised electrons.
1 mark for explaining malleability/ductility by the sliding of layers of cations over one another without shattering.
1 mark for explaining metallic luster through the absorption and reflection/re-emission of incident light by free electrons.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates frequently scored 2 to 3 marks. Electrical conductivity and high melting point were answered well, while the explanation for metallic luster was least understood.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses consistently cited the electron-sea model: delocalised electrons conduct charge, electrostatic attractions between cations and electron sea require high thermal energy to overcome, cation layers slide past each other seamlessly, and oscillating surface electrons reflect light.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses offered circular tautologies like 'they conduct because electricity flows' or 'they are shiny because of their nature' without invoking electrons or lattice structure.
suggestions: Teach the 'positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons' model as the unified framework for explaining all mechanical, electrical, and optical properties of metals.
Conduct structured drills distinguishing between malleability (sheets) and ductility (wires) based on non-directional metallic bonding.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. High melting points: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction hold the positive metal ions and the delocalised electron sea in a giant lattice, requiring large amounts of thermal energy to break.
b. Good electrical conductors: Metals possess free, mobile delocalised electrons that drift towards the positive terminal when a potential difference is applied.
c. Malleable and ductile: When mechanical force is applied, layers of positive metal cations can slide over one another without fracturing the non-directional metallic bond, as mobile electrons adjust instantly.
d. Lustrous: The free delocalised electrons on the metal surface readily absorb incident light energy and immediately re-emit (reflect) it, producing a shiny luster.

questions.questionText:
A compound contains 24% carbon, 12% hydrogen and 64% oxygen by mass. The relative molecular mass of this compound is 50.057 g/mol.
i. Calculate the empirical formula of the given compound. (4 Marks)
ii. Determine its molecular formula. (2 Marks)
(Note: Atomic mass of C = 12 amu, H = 1 amu and O = 16 amu)
questions.sloText: Calculate empirical and molecular formulas from percentage composition and molar mass;
checkingHints: 1 mark for converting mass percentages to moles: C = 24/12 = 2.0; H = 12/1 = 12.0; O = 64/16 = 4.0.
1 mark for dividing by the lowest mole value (2.0) to get ratio 1 : 6 : 2.
2 marks for stating the empirical formula CH6O2.
1 mark for calculating empirical mass (50 g/mol) and finding n = 50.057 / 50 ≈ 1.
1 mark for deducing molecular formula = CH6O2.
questions.overallPerformance: A popular choice with high success rates. Candidates who followed the systematic mole ratio method generally earned full marks.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses displayed clearly labeled tabular steps: Element, % mass, Moles (Mass/Ar), Simplest mole ratio, Empirical formula (CH6O2), followed by empirical mass calculation (50 amu) and determining n = 1 to give molecular formula CH6O2.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses divided percentages directly by atomic numbers rather than atomic masses, or inverted the ratio division step.
suggestions: Enforce a 4-column table for empirical formula calculations: Element | Mass% | Moles | Simplest Ratio.
Remind students that relative atomic masses must be used for mole calculations, not atomic numbers.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Empirical Formula Calculation:
• Moles of C = 24 / 12 = 2.0 mol
• Moles of H = 12 / 1 = 12.0 mol
• Moles of O = 64 / 16 = 4.0 mol

Simplest atomic ratio (divide by 2.0):
• C : 2.0 / 2.0 = 1
• H : 12.0 / 2.0 = 6
• O : 4.0 / 2.0 = 2

Empirical Formula = CH6O2

ii. Molecular Formula Determination:
• Empirical formula mass = (1 * 12) + (6 * 1) + (2 * 16) = 12 + 6 + 32 = 50 g/mol
• n = Molecular Mass / Empirical Mass = 50.057 / 50 ≈ 1
• Molecular Formula = (CH6O2)1 = CH6O2

questions.questionText:
The given graph represents the effect of temperature on the solubility of sodium sulphate.
With reference to this graph, answer the following questions.
i. Identify the approximate minimum and maximum solubility of Na2SO4. (2 Marks)
ii. Interpret the trend of solubility of Na2SO4 depicted in this graph. (2 Marks)
iii. By mentioning the guiding rule of solubility, describe any ONE factor that affects the solubility of any salt. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Interpret solubility curves and describe factors affecting solubility;
checkingHints: 1 mark each for reading minimum (~5 g/100 g H2O) and maximum (~50 g/100 g H2O) solubility values from the graph.
1 mark for explaining steep rise up to ~32.4 °C, and 1 mark for explaining gradual drop above ~32.4 °C.
1 mark for stating 'Like dissolves like' and 1 mark for explaining temperature effect or nature of solute/solvent.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates read values from the graph well. Explaining the dual trend (increase followed by decrease) was challenging for candidates unfamiliar with hydrated versus anhydrous salt behavior.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses accurately extracted values (~5 g at 0 °C and ~50 g at ~32 °C), noted that solubility increases initially due to endothermic dissolution of Na2SO4·10H2O and then decreases as anhydrous Na2SO4 dissolves exothermically, stated 'like dissolves like', and explained temperature dependence.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses overlooked the downward slope after the peak, claiming solubility increases continuously with temperature, or forgot to state the 'like dissolves like' rule in part (iii).
suggestions: Expose students to non-linear solubility curves (such as Na2SO4 and CaSO4) and explain the structural reason (transition from decahydrate to anhydrous salt at 32.4 °C).
Practice graphical reading with units (g of solute per 100 g of water).
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Graph Interpretation:
• Minimum solubility: ~5 g per 100 g of H2O (at 0 °C).
• Maximum solubility: ~50 g per 100 g of H2O (at around 32.4 °C).

ii. Trend Interpretation:
• From 0 °C to approximately 32.4 °C, solubility rises steeply with increasing temperature as hydrated sodium sulphate (Na2SO4·10H2O) dissolves endothermically.
• Above 32.4 °C, the salt loses water of crystallization to become anhydrous Na2SO4, which dissolves exothermically; hence its solubility gently decreases with further temperature rise.

iii. Guiding Rule & Factor:
• Guiding rule: 'Like dissolves like' (polar ionic salts dissolve in polar solvents like water).
• Factor (Temperature): For endothermic dissolutions (ΔH > 0), increasing temperature enhances solubility; for exothermic dissolutions (ΔH < 0), higher temperature reduces solubility.

questions.questionText:
Given are the diagrams of two different molecules, P and Q.
The following table provides information about each element of these molecules.
Element X: Group 5, Period 2
Element Y: Group 1, Period 1
Element Z: Group 7, Period 3

Using the given information, answer the following questions.
i. Identify the molecules, P and Q. (2 Marks)
ii. If molecules P and Q combine chemically, then
   I. draw a dot and cross structure to represent the newly formed compound. (1 Mark)
   II. name the bond that forms between the two molecules and write any TWO specific characteristics of compounds having this bond. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe coordinate covalent bonding and properties of coordinate compounds;
checkingHints: 1 mark each for identifying Molecule P as Ammonia (NH3) and Molecule Q as Hydrogen chloride (HCl).
1 mark for drawing/describing dot-and-cross structure of ammonium chloride [NH4]+ [Cl]-.
1 mark for identifying Coordinate covalent (dative) bond.
2 marks for stating two valid characteristics of coordinate compounds (higher m.p./b.p., polar solubility, directional character).
questions.overallPerformance: Identifying NH3 and HCl from periodic table data was well executed. Drawing the coordinate bond representation in ammonium chloride and explaining properties was answered with varied precision.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses identified X=N, Y=H, Z=Cl, making P=NH3 and Q=HCl. They drew [NH4]+ [Cl]- showing the lone pair on N donated to H+, named the bond as coordinate covalent (dative) bond, and listed two accurate characteristics (polar nature, high melting point compared to simple covalent).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses misidentified elements (e.g., claiming X was Phosphorus or Boron) or simply labeled the bond as ionic or covalent without recognizing coordinate covalent bonding.
suggestions: Train students to identify elements by Group (valence electrons) and Period (energy shells).
Illustrate coordinate covalent bonding clearly using classic donor-acceptor examples like NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl and NH3 + BF3.
questions.currentTopic: Structure of Molecules & Coordinate Covalent Bonding
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Identification:
• Element X (Group 5, Period 2) = Nitrogen (N)
• Element Y (Group 1, Period 1) = Hydrogen (H)
• Element Z (Group 7, Period 3) = Chlorine (Cl)
• Molecule P = NH3 (Ammonia)
• Molecule Q = HCl (Hydrogen chloride)

ii. Chemical Reaction:
I. Dot and Cross Representation:
   When NH3 and HCl react, ammonia's unshared lone pair of electrons is donated to H+ from HCl, forming the ammonium ion [NH4]+ balanced by the chloride ion Cl-:
   [ H : N(H)(H) -> H ]+ [ :Cl: ]-

II. Bond Name & Characteristics:
• Bond Name: Coordinate Covalent (Dative) Bond.
• Characteristics:
  1. Higher melting and boiling points than non-polar covalent compounds due to semi-polar nature.
  2. Soluble in polar solvents like water and conduct electricity in molten or aqueous state.

questions.questionText:
Given below is the image of a zinc-carbon battery.
i. What is the anode and cathode made up of in the given dry cell battery? (2 Marks)
ii. How does the zinc-carbon battery work? Support your answer using balanced chemical equations for the reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode. (4 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the construction, working, and chemical reactions of a dry cell (zinc-carbon battery);
checkingHints: 1 mark each for Anode (Zinc casing/container) and Cathode (Carbon/graphite rod surrounded by MnO2).
2 marks for explaining working: zinc oxidation at anode, electron flow through circuit, reduction of MnO2 at cathode.
1 mark for balanced anode half-equation: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-.
1 mark for balanced cathode half-equation: 2MnO2 + 2NH4+ + 2e- -> Mn2O3 + 2NH3 + H2O.
questions.overallPerformance: Most candidates knew that zinc forms the outer casing and carbon forms the central rod. Writing the balanced half-reactions with MnO2 and NH4Cl was the primary discriminator.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses precisely defined the anode as the zinc container and cathode as graphite/MnO2, described the spontaneous redox reaction driving current through the external circuit, and provided accurate balanced half-reactions for oxidation and reduction.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses reversed anode and cathode polarities, omitted MnO2, or wrote incomplete, unbalanced chemical equations.
suggestions: Use cross-sectional dry cell models in the laboratory to demonstrate physical components (zinc can, graphite rod, separator, electrolyte paste).
Practice writing and balancing half-reactions for common electrochemical commercial cells.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Electrodes in Dry Cell:
• Anode (-): Zinc (Zn) outer container / casing.
• Cathode (+): Graphite (carbon) rod packed in a paste of manganese dioxide (MnO2) and carbon powder.

ii. Working and Chemical Reactions:
• Working: Zinc undergoes spontaneous oxidation at the anode, releasing electrons that travel through the external circuit to deliver electric power. At the cathode, manganese dioxide is reduced in the presence of ammonium ions from the wet electrolyte paste (NH4Cl + ZnCl2).
• Anode Reaction (Oxidation):
  Zn(s) -> Zn2+(aq) + 2e-
• Cathode Reaction (Reduction):
  2MnO2(s) + 2NH4+(aq) + 2e- -> Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(aq) + H2O(l)
• Overall Reaction:
  Zn(s) + 2MnO2(s) + 2NH4Cl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(aq) + H2O(l)
